item.title: Imagine There Was No Naturalistic Decision-Making Movement
item.description:
Decision-Making

Imagine There Was No Naturalistic Decision-Making Movement

A counterfactual exercise to gauge the impact of naturalistic decision-making.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • It is easy to imagine that the Naturalistic Decision-Making movement never got started.
  • It is also easy to imagine the impact in so many communities of not having an NDM framework.
  • This counterfactual exercise was a useful method for appreciating what NDM has contributed.

The Naturalistic Decision-Making movement just celebrated its 40th anniversary at the 18th NDM meeting in Charlottesville, Virginia, in June 2026.

Afterwards I ran a counterfactual exercise with some colleagues to capture what the Naturalistic Decision-Making (NDM) movement has contributed to the field of psychology. The exercise was valuable for highlighting the value added of NDM. It was also valuable as a tactic for using counterfactuals.

Here is a partial list of what we came up with:

  1. Balkanization. Practitioners in various fields would develop their own naturalistic models of decision-making.
  2. Gap. There would be a larger gap between work as imagined vs. work as done. And there would be less support for looking at work as it is actually done.
  3. Fatalities. According to what we have heard from first responders and related professionals such as emergency department physicians, without NDM there would be more fatalities in high-risk domains such as firefighting and healthcare.
  4. Expertise. Our understanding of expertise would be severely limited; experts would be disrespected.
  5. The cognitive dimension. There would be less familiarity with the cognitive dimension in the practitioner communities. Tactics in these fields would be more focused on procedures, as opposed to the cognitive dimension.
  6. Doctrine regarding military decision making. Without NDM, the military decision-making process in the Army (Military Decision Making Process) would likely still be in effect, without any consideration for expertise-based rapid decisions.
  7. Research methods. The academic-led embargo on field research would be in force. Laboratory-oriented traditions would hold sway, making it difficult for researchers to break free from the rigid experimental approaches. As a result, there would be a lack of methods for examining sense-making and decision making in naturalistic settings (e.g., using cognitive task analysis).
  8. Training and design. We would not have a great understanding of how to train tacit knowledge or design systems to support it. Our limited understanding of what expertise truly is would inhibit our interventions. There would be fewer scenario/simulation-based training opportunities.
  9. Discoveries. There would have been fewer discoveries of macrocognitive phenomena such as sense-making, problem detection, and insight.

So, it's a pretty grim picture, if our counterfactual exercise is to be believed. This exercise has helped us appreciate what the NDM community has contributed to our research and our training and design approaches.

I thank the following colleagues who contributed their ideas: Robert Hoffman, Joseph Borders, John Schmitt, Emily Newsome, Jared Peterson, Katrina Carlson, Kari Hoy, Micah Condon and Laura Militello.

item.title: Coercive Control Laws: What's Missing?
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

Coercive Control Laws: What's Missing?

When psychological abuse is overlooked, it undermines its serious harm.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Coercive control laws to address intimate partner abuse exist in 10 states.
  • Addressing coercive control in intimate relationships is an important step toward protecting survivors.
  • What is missing is the inclusion of psychological abuse, which can be more harmful and entrapping.
Source: Tumisu/Pixabay

Intimate partner abuse, termed in the legal realm as coercive control, has been recognized by 10 states making coercive control illegal. However, some differences exist with what the coercive control law includes and the coercive controlling experience by an intimate partner. The psychologically abusive aspects of coercive control in an intimate relationship are not recognized in the law and remain unregulated. Yet, this aspect of intimate partner abuse is traumatically damaging and might be the most entrapping aspect of intimate partner abuse.

When a coercive control law identifies behaviors and not tactics of psychological abuse, the serious harm of psychological abuse gets overlooked.

Coercive Control Laws

Coercive control laws identified by WomensLaw (2025) include behaviors such as:

  • Isolating someone from family, friends, or support networks.
  • Controlling finances, profitable resources, or access to work opportunities.
  • Monitoring daily activities, behaviors, or electronic communications.
  • Depriving someone of basic needs, sleep, or medical attention.
  • Threats of harm to children, relatives, or pets.

These are serious and harmful behaviors intended to dominate and control that grossly undermines a partner’s autonomy. They are also behaviors that are recognizable and measurable, perhaps more likely for someone to reveal evidence that coercive control exists in the relationship. This is tremendous progress in protecting those enduring this aspect of coercive abuse.

Psychological Harm

Psychological abuse of an intimate partner undermines one’s freedom in a very different way than recognized in the new laws of coercive control. Psychological abuse harms with hidden injuries that are not easily seen. Coercive tactics of control impact one’s life dramatically because they target a person’s thoughts, feelings, and perception—how they see things, a sense of self, view of the relationship and connection with the surrounding world. Often these subtle and difficult-to-identify tactics are often not readily seen by the recipient unless they know what they are.

article continues after advertisement

Working with survivors of controlling partners in recovery, I hear over and over two profound losses that are endured—loss of trust in their own perception and judgment, and more encompassing, a loss of self. Many women who are mothers painfully identify from this transformed place, that they are not the mother they want to be. At the outset of recovery, the survivor doesn’t know how this harm occurred but they do sense a deep sadness and grief of what they lost along the way.

Recognizing Coercive Tactics of Psychological Abuse for Recovery

The gradual undermining by a coercive partner of a survivor’s well-being by degradation, gaslighting, blaming, etc. creates a damaging entrapment. The best protection for one’s self is trauma recovery. The first step to dismantle the entrapment is identifying the coercive tactics embedded in their partner’s behaviors. Also, seeing how each coercive tactic holds an intended psychological impact in the service of overpowering the victim.

As survivors unpack their abusive experience, they are dismantling their entrapment and can begin to see their coercive partner realistically. This process of recovery is reconnecting with a sense of self, feeling whole again, and gaining confidence in trusting their own perception. When this is accomplished, and often only then, survivors are able to determine what they need to do going forward.
